newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau Chinese pupils protest over disputed islands.
newsitem.headline: Macau Chinese pupils protest over disputed islands.

text.p: School bells tolled across Macau on Wednesday and pupils rallied in schoolyards to protest against Japan's claim to a disputed group of islands.

Marking the 65th anniversary of Japan's invasion of China, schools jointly counting more than 20,000 pupils rallied their entire rolls in their yards for special lessons on "Japanese militarism and expansionism".
About one-third of the schools in this Portuguese-ruled territory belong to a Chinese Education Association.

Big Chinese-character posters hung from the walls of many buildings, demanding that Japan respect China's sovereignty over the disputed East China Sea islands which China refers to as the Diaoyu isles, while Japan calls them the Senkaku group.

Anti-Japan protests in Chinese-populated territories have been steadily growing over the past month, sparked by Japan's renewed claim to the uninhabited archipelago and the actions of rightwing Japanese who erected a lighthouse there.

The issue is a common rallying cry among the 62 candidates and 12 political groups contesting Macau's legislative elections on Sunday. The poll is the last for the Legislative Assembly before Macau, ruled by Portugal for almost five centuries, is handed back to Beijing in December 1999.
Pro-democracy groups in Macau, a small territory consisting of a peninsula that juts off the southern tip of China and two islands, have called for a boycott of Japanese goods.

The 424,000-strong population is 95 percent ethnic Chinese, and many people have bitter memories of Japan's 1931 invasion of northern China and subsequent 14-year-long military carve-up of the country, accompanied by a string of atrocities.
A Macau sports club said on Wednesday that 30 of its members planned to sail to the disputed islands within the next few weeks in another protest.
Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories.
Chinese historians point to maps that show China has possessed the islands for centuries.
